title: Vayigash: does my father live? (Genesis 45:3)
hook: Joseph's first words after "I am Joseph" are about his father
tomorrow: Vayigash: don't fall out on the way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah drew near and offered himself in place of his youngest brother. Your line was draw near. Today, the man he was pleading with breaks.

Judah has just finished speaking. He's described an old man at home who will die of grief if the youngest son doesn't come back. And the ruler of Egypt can't hold it in anymore. He clears the room: everyone out. The servants go. Now it's only him and his brothers. He cries so loudly the Egyptians hear it through the walls. Then he says two sentences. The first is the line people know. The second one is today.

In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" In Hebrew it's five words. Ani Yosef, I am Joseph. Ha'od avi chai, is my father still alive? The brothers can't answer; they're terrified in front of him. Here's the puzzle the rabbis loved. Joseph already knows the answer: Judah's whole speech was about their living father. So why ask? One answer: it isn't a question for information. It's the first thing out of a son who hasn't seen his father since the day he was sold. The power, the grain, the revenge he could take all fall away, and what's left is: Dad. Is he really alive? Another answer is sharper. Some readers hear a rebuke underneath. You talk about our father's grief, Judah? Where was that concern the day you sold me? A midrash says that when the brothers couldn't answer this one question, a sage later sighed: if a brother's words left them speechless, how will any of us answer on the day we're asked about our own lives? Both readings can be true at once. Then Joseph says, come near to me, please. The same verb as yesterday. Judah drew near to plead; now Joseph asks all of them to draw near to be forgiven. The first thing a lost son asks about is the parent. Joseph waited years to ask it out loud. Some people wait longer than they meant to.
screen: `I AM JOSEPH.` · `IS MY FATHER STILL ALIVE?` · `A CRY, OR A REBUKE?` · `COME NEAR TO ME, PLEASE.` · then, large: `DOTH MY FATHER YET LIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one older person who shaped you: a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, an old neighbor, and picture their face. Ask Joseph's question in your own words: how are they, really? If they're living, decide when you'll call; if they've died, let yourself remember one thing they used to say.
Vayigash. The portion where Joseph finally says I am Joseph, and his very next words ask after his father.
Your line: doth my father yet live. Under all that power, he was still a son. Rest well.

howItsDone: Honoring father and mother is one of the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in practical ways: providing for aging parents, standing when they enter, not contradicting them harshly, and saying Kaddish for them after they die.

original.note: Hebrew: is my father still alive? Joseph's words right after I am Joseph (Genesis 45:3).

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph wanted news from home.
what it means: a son's first cry after all those years, and maybe a rebuke, since Judah had just described their father.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah draws a lesson from the brothers' silence: if they couldn't answer Joseph's rebuke, how will anyone answer God's?

chat.says: Why would Joseph ask if his father was alive? Judah had just told him.
options: A son's first cry after years apart, or a quiet rebuke, or both at once.
He hadn't been listening to Judah's speech, so he truly didn't know.
He asked to stall, because he wasn't ready to say who he was.
chat.meaning: Joseph already knew. The rabbis hear a son's longing, is Dad really alive?, and some hear a rebuke: where was that concern when you sold me?

Ha'od avi chai.meaning: Hebrew: is my father still alive?

Vayigash.meaning: and he drew near; the name of this week's portion

midrash.meaning: a rabbinic teaching that fills a gap in the text

sources.quoted: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?

notes: The midrash about the brothers' silence and the day of rebuke (attributed to Abba Kohen Bardela) is cited from memory as Genesis Rabbah 93:10; confirm reference and paraphrase.
'Over twenty years' apart: Joseph sold at 17 (37:2), stands before Pharaoh at 30 (41:46), plus seven years of plenty and two of famine (45:6), about 22 years; confirm.
The 'rebuke' reading is one of several commentators' readings; a Keeper may want it attributed to a named commentator.
